People ask me how long it takes to set up in the United States, and I always give the same unhelpful answer: the company takes a morning and the rest takes a year. Incorporating is genuinely quick. The filings are made online, the certificate arrives, and everybody feels wonderful for about a week. Then you need a bank account, and the account is subject to checks that were written for money laundering, not for a media company from Sao Paulo with no American history. Nothing you say makes that faster. What makes it faster is having an American director, a real address that is not a mailbox, and a track record you can show on paper. My advice is boring and it is the only advice that works: start the banking on day one, in parallel with everything else, and assume it will be the thing that decides your launch date.

If I did it again, I would do one thing differently, and it is not the lawyers or the structure. I would refuse to launch in more than one state. We rolled out in four at once because it felt like ambition, and what we actually bought was four sets of payroll rules, four filing calendars and four different answers to the same question. We were not scaling. We were repeating the same small problem in four places and calling it growth. The foothold we eventually got came from a single client in a single state who agreed to be a reference, and everything after that was easier, because for the first time we had something to point at. Go small on purpose. It looks like caution from the outside, and from the inside it is the fastest route there is.

The company decides that the United States is the next market. A subsidiary is incorporated in Delaware, because the company law there is predictable. The filings are made online in a morning, and then the bank account takes months. Payroll, contracts and certification turn out to follow a different rulebook in every state. The operation is only scaled after the same thing has been sold twice to somebody outside the founder's circle.
